## Why this unit matters

Measure more than successful HTTP responses. Use JMeter concepts, Little's law and an interactive workload experiment to reason about bottlenecks.

The same shop remains the anchor: Product owns catalogue information, User owns customer information, and Order coordinates checkout. Read each chapter in order to see which new requirement motivates the next design decision.

## Lessons

1. **[JMeter: Load Testing Basics](jmeter-basics.qmd)**
2. **[Analysing High Load](high-load-analysis.qmd)**
3. **[Interactive Queueing Experiment](interactive-queue-lab.qmd)**

## Learning objective

After this unit, describe the dependency or operational problem **before** naming a framework; draw the relevant call/event path; state the failure mode and trade-off; and explain how the concept applies to a small TypeScript or NestJS service.

## Mathematical Abstraction

Use arrival rate, throughput, and mean response time to reason about average in-flight work.

$$
L=\lambda W
$$

This is Little's law under stable flow and consistent measurement boundaries; it does not determine tail latency by itself.
